questions.q: Why doesn't a brute-force (exact scan) search work well at large scale?
options: It only works with text data, never with vectors
Its cost grows directly with the number of stored vectors — a million vectors means a million comparisons per query
It requires a distance metric, unlike indexed search
It can only run on a single vendor's hardware
questions.explain: A brute-force scan compares the query to every stored vector, so its cost scales linearly with collection size — fine for a few thousand vectors, too slow for millions.

questions.q: In IVF (Inverted File index), what does the `nprobe` parameter control?
options: Higher nprobe = probe more clusters: better recall, but slower queries
The total number of vectors allowed in the entire collection
The distance metric used to compare vectors
How many layers the HNSW graph builds
questions.explain: nprobe sets how many of the nearest cluster centroids get searched at query time — raising it improves recall at the cost of query speed, and lowering it does the opposite.

questions.q: What happens at build time for an IVF index?
options: Every vector is connected into a multi-layer graph
Vectors are grouped into nlist clusters, typically using something like k-means, each with a centroid
A relational table is created with one row per vector
Vectors are sorted alphabetically by their original text
questions.explain: IVF's build step clusters the vector space ahead of time so that, at query time, the search can skip straight to the handful of clusters nearest the query instead of scanning everything.

questions.q: In HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), how does a search generally proceed?
options: It assigns every vector to one of nlist clusters first
It converts every vector into text before comparing
It skips indexing entirely and always does an exact scan
It starts at a sparse top layer and greedily descends toward denser layers, narrowing in on the query at each step
questions.explain: HNSW builds a layered graph — sparse with long-range links at the top, dense with every vector at the bottom — and a search greedily moves toward the closest connected node, dropping a layer each time it can't get any closer.

questions.q: Why are HNSW and IVF both described as "approximate" nearest-neighbor search?
options: Because they only work with embeddings under 128 dimensions
Because they are experimental and not used in production vector databases
They trade a small, tunable amount of accuracy for a much larger gain in query speed, compared to an exact brute-force scan
Because neither one lets you configure a distance metric
questions.explain: Both narrow the search space (IVF via clusters, HNSW via a graph) instead of checking every vector, so they can occasionally miss the true closest match in exchange for being dramatically faster — the same trade-off Lesson 10 introduced as ANN search.
